opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the parts of the model we've found hardest to make progress on.

I think there are a few reasons. The first is that attention is fundamentally about moving information around. An MLP layer at a given position is doing a computation on what's already there, so you can ask, "what features go in and what comes out?" Attention is doing something relational. It's deciding which earlier tokens to look at, and then what information to copy from them. So you really have two questions bundled together: *where* is the model looking, and *what* is it moving. Those are governed by different parts of the computation, the query-key side and the value-output side, and you have to understand both to say anything meaningful.

The second reason is that people often look at attention patterns, those heat maps of which token attends to which, and assume that tells you what the model is doing. It's tempting, because it's very visual. But an attention pattern alone can be pretty misleading. A head might attend strongly to a token and move almost nothing useful, or attend weakly and move something critical. And a lot of heads attend to things like the first token or punctuation as a kind of default "no-op" sink. So the most obvious thing to look at isn't necessarily the most informative.

Third, there's a lot of superposition and distribution going on. You'd love it if each head did one clean job, like the classic induction head that copies the next token after a previous occurrence. Some heads are like that. But many heads seem to do several things depending on context, and many behaviors are spread across multiple heads and layers working together. So the unit you'd naturally want to analyze, the individual head, often isn't the right unit.

And finally, from a tooling perspective, a lot of our recent methods, like replacing the MLPs with more interpretable sparse components and building attribution graphs, work really well for the MLP side. In much of that work, we've often frozen the attention patterns and treated them as given. That lets you trace how features flow through the model, but it means you're explaining the computation *conditional* on where attention went, without explaining *why* it went there. That "why" is often exactly where the interesting stuff is. Things like: how does the model figure out which earlier entity a pronoun refers to, or which piece of the context is relevant for this question.

So I'd say attention isn't uninterpretable in principle. We have some really nice case studies. But it's relational, distributed, and our best current tools somewhat sidestep it, and I think closing that gap is one of the more important open problems in the field.

r001.rationale: The response says, “attention isn’t uninterpretable in principle,” clearly communicating that the difficulty is not a fundamental barrier.

r002.rationale: It does not identify interactions between all query and key positions or explain a resulting quadratic computational cost.

r003.rationale: It notes that attention patterns can mislead, but does not explain how attention’s nonlinearity can suppress a key’s influence when another key is much stronger.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a great question, and I think there are a few layers to it. The first thing I'd say is that attention is kind of seductive, right? Because it's one of the only parts of a transformer that produces something that looks like it's meant to be read by a human. You get this matrix of weights, you can plot it as a heatmap, and you see that token A is "looking at" token B, and it feels like you've opened the hood and you're seeing the engine. And that's where a lot of the early interpretability work on transformers went, for understandable reasons.

The problem is that the attention pattern is really only half the story, and arguably the less important half. Attention tells you where information is being moved from and to, but it doesn't tell you what information is being moved, or what the model does with it once it gets there. That's determined by the value and output projections and then everything downstream in the MLPs and later layers. So you can have two heads with identical attention patterns that are doing completely different things computationally, and you'd never know it from the heatmap alone.

The second issue is that attention weights aren't really faithful explanations in the way people want them to be. There's a bunch of work showing you can perturb attention pretty substantially and the model's output barely changes, or conversely that the tokens with the highest attention aren't the ones that actually matter if you go and do an ablation. So the thing that looks like an explanation isn't necessarily tracking what's causally driving the behavior.

And then the third thing, which I think is the deepest one, is that attention operates on the residual stream, and the residual stream is this dense, superposed representation where a single direction can mean many things depending on context. So even if you knew exactly which positions a head was reading from, you'd still have to answer the question of what features are present at those positions, and that's not something you can read off directly. It's why a lot of the more recent work, at Anthropic and elsewhere, has moved toward trying to decompose those activations into interpretable features first, and then asking how attention and the MLPs move and transform those features. Once you have a vocabulary for what the model is representing, the attention patterns become a lot more legible, because now you can say "this head is moving the 'this is a name' feature to the position where the model needs to decide whether to copy it," instead of just "this head attends to earlier tokens."

So I don't think attention is uninterpretable. I think it's just that we were trying to interpret it in isolation, and it turns out it's a piece of a circuit, and you need the rest of the circuit to make sense of it.

r001.rationale: The response says attention is not inherently uninterpretable and explains that interpreting it alongside the rest of the circuit and represented features can make it more legible.

r002.rationale: It does not identify interactions between query and key positions or quadratic computational cost as an interpretability difficulty.

r003.rationale: It does not explain how attention’s nonlinearity can reduce one key’s influence when another key is much stronger.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that an attention weight tells you something about how information is being routed, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what that information means or how it affects the final prediction. You can look at a visualization and say, “This word is attending to that word,” and that feels like an explanation. But what computation is actually happening there?

Especially as you stack layers, the representations being passed around are no longer just representations of individual words. They’ve already incorporated information from other parts of the sequence. And you have multiple heads doing this simultaneously, with other computations happening between attention layers.

So attention gives you a useful window into the model, but there’s a gap between observing a strong attention weight and saying, “This is why the model produced this answer.” To make that stronger claim, you’d want to intervene—change or remove something—and see whether the output changes in the way your explanation predicts.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between attention weights and explanations, but does not say these difficulties are not fundamental barriers.

r002.rationale: It mentions multiple heads and stacked layers, but not interactions between all query and key positions or their quadratic interpretation cost.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that attention nonlinearity can suppress a key’s influence when another key is much stronger.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that attention gives you something that looks like an explanation. You can visualize it and say, “When the model produced this word, it was paying attention to those words.” That’s intuitive, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you why the model made that prediction.

An attention weight describes one part of a computation. What information is actually being passed depends on the representations being weighted, and then you have many heads and many layers interacting. So a high attention weight doesn’t automatically mean that a particular word was important to the final answer.

The distinction is between seeing a pattern and establishing that it explains the behavior. To get at the latter, you need to intervene—change an input or a component of the model—and see whether the prediction changes in the way your explanation would suggest. Attention visualizations can be useful clues, but they’re not a complete explanation on their own.

r001.rationale: The response notes limits of attention visualizations but does not say these interpretability difficulties are not fundamental barriers.
